calibration_source: Eurostat (namq_10_gdp, namq_10_pe, namq_10_a10_e, demo_pjanbroad, lfsi_emp_a), OECD LFS, ECB

x_comments.alpha_K: Capital share set to 0.33 for cross-country comparability with Germany and Poland, both of which use 0.33 in the Ramsey layer. PWT labsh for Spain implies alpha nearer 0.38-0.40, but holding alpha_K fixed across countries keeps the Ramsey trends comparable and avoids a BGP K/Y that diverges from the other two models for a purely measurement-driven reason.
x_comments.delta_annual: 5% annual depreciation for total-economy capital, matching Germany rather than Poland's 6%. Spain's capital stock is unusually structures-heavy after the 1998-2007 construction boom, and structures depreciate slowly; the growth model matches total GFCF (Eurostat P51G) including those structures, so the lower rate is the right one.
x_comments.beta_annual: Discount factor: 0.96 annual, same as Germany and Poland. It pins the terminal modified-golden-rule BGP real rate jointly with sigma and terminal_growth.g_A_terminal_annual; the resulting r* is written to output/documentation_data/ramsey/ramsey_summary_Spain.json (structural.r_star_annual) by calibrate_growth_model rather than quoted here, because it is derived and would go stale.
x_comments.sigma: Inverse IES (CRRA coefficient). sigma=1.5 is mid-range consensus (1=log, 2=high risk aversion), same as Germany and Poland.
x_comments.tfp_growth_annual: 0.4% annual labour-augmenting TFP growth, set by the rule g_A = g_(Y/(N h)) * (1 - alpha_K), with g_(Y/(N h)) the growth of GDP per hour worked: on a BGP where K grows with Y, output per hour grows at g_A / (1 - alpha_K). On the current levels data (2000q1-2025q1, all persons in employment and hours per person employed) GDP per hour worked grows 0.68% p.a. (first against last four quarters), so the rule gives 0.68% * 0.67 = 0.46%. The rule value is not used because it does not improve the trend: at 0.4% the trend's output per hour already grows 0.70% p.a., as fast as the data, while 0.46% makes it grow 0.77% and lowers corr(y_ramsey, y_hp) from 0.73 to 0.72 (measured 2026-11-09). This is close to Germany's 0.53% and consistent with the well-documented stagnation of Spanish TFP over this period. It is deliberately NOT set to zero: measured Spanish TFP growth is near zero over 2000-2013 and recovers after, and a zero or negative trend would give a degenerate BGP. Revisit if the sample is extended. The forward path converges to the common terminal_growth rate (see that block).

base_year_values.x_comment: calibrate_growth_model.m writes calibrated base-year levels and derived fields into input/ES/MacroModel/growth_params_Spain.json.

inflation_target.x_comment: ECB 2% target - Spain is a euro founder member, so the same target as Germany applies for the whole 2000q1 sample. Differs from Poland's 2.5% NBP target. pi_star entered as annual percent.

labor_trends.nawru_source: PLACEHOLDER: HP trend (lambda=160000) of the in-sample ILO unemployment rate, written by calibrate_growth_model.m. Intended source: AMECO.
labor_trends.demographic_L_source: PLACEHOLDER: HP trend (lambda=160000) of the in-sample labour force, written by calibrate_growth_model.m; no projection tail. Intended source: Eurostat population projections + INE labor force participation.
labor_trends.demographic_P_source: Up to the SimPaths handoff quarter: HP trend (lambda=160000) of the resident population (pop_level, census breaks spliced in the data stage), written by calibrate_growth_model.m. After it: growth path of SimPaths align_popProjections.xlsx (all ages), written by build_population_projection.m.
labor_trends.x_comment: nawru_file is read for diagnostics only. demographic_L_file has no post-sample tail, so ramsey_trend.m extends N at its trailing 20-quarter trend growth rate, untapered, until build_population_projection.m supplies a projection. Hours: log-linear trend fitted to observed. The planner reads demographic_P_file in full and holds P/N at its last value beyond it.

solver.x_comment: Stacked-time Newton (LBJ) perfect-foresight solver with terminal K/Y closure. 400 terminal quarters (~100 years) as for Germany, Sweden and the UK; the terminal_growth path has converged long before their end (rho_quarterly^400 is about 1e-6). Newton convergence requires ||F||_inf <= 1.0e-10 within 200 iterations.

terminal_growth.x_comment: Forward TFP growth starts at tfp_growth_annual and converges quarter by quarter to g_A_terminal_annual, g_t = g_term + rho_quarterly * (g_(t-1) - g_term). All five countries share g_A_terminal_annual = 0.5% and rho_quarterly = 0.966, a half-life of 5 years. The in-sample rate is measured per country; the long run is a common assumption, because TFP growth decades ahead is unknown and convergence to a common rate is the neutral one. 0.5% is the conservative value: it implies long-run growth of output per hour of 0.75% a year (g_A / (1 - alpha_K)). The half-life keeps a catch-up rate from carrying far into the projection: it puts Poland's forward trend wage growth (2023q1-2059q4) at about 1.6% a year (measured 2026-11-09), close to the trend in vanilla SimPaths' wage equation (about 1.5% a year). The in-sample solve holds tfp_growth_annual through the last data quarter; the forward solve converges from the handoff quarter.
